title: Swift Foundations
description: Mobile-first Swift practice for language fluency, SwiftUI judgment, and interview confidence.

courses.title: Swift for Mobile Engineers
courses.description: Build the mental models behind safe, readable Swift before reaching for a full IDE.

chapters.title: Unit 1 · Swift foundations
chapters.summary: Values, types, optionals, structs, enums, and control flow.

lessons.title: Think in Swift values
lessons.explanation: Swift rewards explicit, value-oriented code. Learn the choices that make a small mobile feature easier to trust.

exercises.prompt: Which keyword declares a binding that cannot be reassigned?
exercises.explanation: Use let for a binding that should not be reassigned after initialization.

exercises.prompt: What does the question mark in String? mean?
options: The value is optional and may be nil
exercises.explanation: A question mark creates an Optional, which can hold a value or nil.

exercises.prompt: Which construct is best for unwrapping an optional and exiting early when it is nil?
exercises.explanation: guard let keeps the happy path unwrapped and makes the failure exit explicit.

exercises.prompt: What is a struct in Swift primarily used for?
options: A value type that groups data and behavior
exercises.explanation: Structs are value types and are a common default for modeling app data.

exercises.prompt: Which type is useful when a value should be one of a closed set of cases?
exercises.explanation: An enum models a finite set of states and lets the compiler help with exhaustive handling.

exercises.prompt: Why is exhaustive switch handling valuable?
options: It forces every known state to be considered
exercises.explanation: Exhaustive switches make new enum cases visible at compile time instead of silently ignored.

exercises.prompt: What does type inference allow Swift to do?
options: Infer a value's type from context
exercises.explanation: Swift can infer many types while still checking them statically.

exercises.prompt: Which choice is safer than force-unwrapping an optional in production code?
options: Use guard let or if let
exercises.explanation: Optional binding handles the absence case explicitly instead of crashing when nil appears.

chapters.title: Unit 2 · Collections
chapters.summary: Use arrays, dictionaries, sets, and transformations with clear intent.

lessons.title: Shape data with collections
lessons.explanation: Collection choice is a reasoning decision: preserve order, look up by key, or remove duplicates.

exercises.prompt: Which collection preserves order and allows duplicate values?
exercises.explanation: Array is the ordered collection that can contain duplicate elements.

exercises.prompt: Which collection is designed for unique values?
exercises.explanation: Set stores unique values and is useful for membership checks and de-duplication.

exercises.prompt: What is the best collection for looking up a user by an id?
exercises.explanation: Dictionary maps keys to values, making keyed lookup the clearest model.

exercises.prompt: Which transformation keeps only elements matching a condition?
exercises.explanation: filter returns the elements for which the predicate is true.

exercises.prompt: Which transformation changes every element into a new value?
exercises.explanation: map applies a transform to each element and returns the transformed collection.

exercises.prompt: What is reduce commonly used for?
options: Combine elements into one accumulated result
exercises.explanation: reduce folds a collection into a single value such as a sum or grouped result.

exercises.prompt: Why can Swift arrays behave like value types?
options: They cannot be passed to functions
exercises.explanation: Copy-on-write value semantics provide predictable ownership while avoiding unnecessary copies.

exercises.prompt: Which operation is a good first choice when you need sorted display data without mutating the source?
exercises.explanation: sorted returns a new ordered collection; sort mutates a mutable collection in place.

chapters.title: Unit 3 · Concurrency
chapters.summary: Recognize async work, actors, cancellation, and main-thread UI updates.

lessons.title: Make async work understandable
lessons.explanation: Concurrency is about isolating work and describing when a value is available, not about sprinkling threads everywhere.

exercises.prompt: Which keyword marks a function that can suspend while waiting?
exercises.explanation: async declares that a function may suspend and be called with await.

exercises.prompt: What does await communicate at a call site?
options: The call may suspend until a result is ready
The call always runs on the main thread
The call is guaranteed to fail
exercises.explanation: await makes suspension points visible where asynchronous work may pause.

exercises.prompt: What problem does an actor help prevent?
options: Unsafe concurrent access to isolated mutable state
exercises.explanation: Actors serialize access to their isolated state and help prevent data races.

exercises.prompt: Which annotation is commonly used for UI-bound observable state?
exercises.explanation: @MainActor documents and enforces that the isolated work belongs on the main actor.

exercises.prompt: Why should async work check for cancellation?
options: A cancelled screen should stop wasting work
It removes the need for errors
exercises.explanation: Cancellation lets work exit when the user no longer needs its result.

exercises.prompt: What is async let useful for?
options: Starting independent async work that can be awaited later
exercises.explanation: async let makes independent child tasks explicit so their results can be awaited together.

exercises.prompt: Which error-handling shape fits an async operation that can throw?
exercises.explanation: A throwing async call combines the two effects as try await.

exercises.prompt: What is a good default for a cancelled image request?
options: Ignore its result and release its resources
Block the UI until it finishes
exercises.explanation: Cancellation should be treated as a normal lifecycle outcome when a result is no longer relevant.

chapters.title: Unit 4 · SwiftUI
chapters.summary: Understand views, state flow, bindings, lists, navigation, and accessibility.

lessons.title: Build a calm SwiftUI screen
lessons.explanation: SwiftUI works best when the view describes state and lets data flow predictably through the hierarchy.

exercises.prompt: What is the body property of a SwiftUI View?
options: A description of the view hierarchy
exercises.explanation: body describes what SwiftUI should render for the current state.

exercises.prompt: Which wrapper is appropriate for simple local view state?
exercises.explanation: @State stores local state owned by the view.

exercises.prompt: What does a Binding provide?
options: A two-way connection to state owned elsewhere
exercises.explanation: Binding lets a child read and write state owned by a parent or model.

exercises.prompt: Which view is a natural choice for repeated rows of data?
exercises.explanation: List is optimized for displaying repeated, scrollable rows.

exercises.prompt: Why does ForEach need stable identity for dynamic data?
options: SwiftUI can diff and update the right rows
exercises.explanation: Stable identity helps SwiftUI understand what changed between renders.

exercises.prompt: What should an accessible button communicate beyond its visual label?
exercises.explanation: Assistive technology needs a clear action and context, not just decorative styling.

exercises.prompt: Which container is designed for stack-based navigation in modern SwiftUI?
exercises.explanation: NavigationStack models a navigation path and pushes destinations predictably.

exercises.prompt: What is the most useful mental model for a SwiftUI view?
options: A function of state that can be recomputed
exercises.explanation: Views are lightweight descriptions derived from state, so recomputation is expected.

chapters.title: Unit 5 · Interview patterns
chapters.summary: Explain complexity, boundaries, testing, and the simplest correct approach.

lessons.title: Reason before you code
lessons.explanation: Interview confidence comes from naming the invariant, the edge cases, and the trade-off before writing syntax.

exercises.prompt: What should you clarify before implementing an interview problem?
options: Input, output, constraints, and edge cases
exercises.explanation: A clear contract prevents solving the wrong problem and gives you test cases to discuss.

exercises.prompt: What is the average lookup complexity of a hash table?
exercises.explanation: Hash tables provide average constant-time lookup when hashing remains well distributed.

exercises.prompt: When is a two-pointer approach especially useful?
options: Walking a sequence from two coordinated positions
exercises.explanation: Two pointers are useful for sorted arrays, windows, and coordinated scans.

exercises.prompt: What is a base case in recursion?
options: The condition that stops further recursive calls
exercises.explanation: Without a base case, recursive calls do not have a defined stopping point.

exercises.prompt: Which test is most valuable for a boundary-focused solution?
options: An empty or smallest valid input
exercises.explanation: Smallest and empty inputs expose off-by-one and missing-state errors early.

exercises.prompt: What makes a solution easier to review?
options: A named invariant and focused helpers
exercises.explanation: Naming the invariant and separating decisions makes correctness easier to inspect.

exercises.prompt: When should you prefer the simplest correct algorithm over premature optimization?
options: When constraints do not require the extra complexity
Whenever a variable is named result
exercises.explanation: Complexity has a maintenance cost; optimize in response to constraints and evidence.

exercises.prompt: What is a strong way to communicate complexity?
options: State time and space costs and why they arise
exercises.explanation: A concise explanation connects the algorithm's operations to its time and space costs.
